preamble: Eight characters are of a kind and may lack further definition.

clue.text: First third or fifth of the over? Curious

definitions.text: First third or fifth of the over
definitions.note: a noun phrase for a delivery; the answer read as two words, odd ball
definitions.meaning: a cricket over has six deliveries, and the first, third and fifth are the odd-numbered balls

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is six balls bowled in a row; numbers one, three and five are odd balls. The single word is then a slang adjective for someone peculiar.
explanation.definitionFit: Oddball is informal for an eccentric or peculiar person or thing, which is what curious means here: strange rather than inquisitive.

clue.text: Turn to fossil (if fifty were unknown)

definitions.text: Turn to fossil (if fifty were unknown)

indicators.note: to turn something is to twist it round, so the letters get rearranged
the bracket imagines a world where one letter stood for another, so we swap it

parts.note: taken as written
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
x, y and z are the unknowns in algebra

explanation.surface: A note about fossilisation with an odd mathematical aside in brackets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' does double duty: it is part of the definition and also the signal to rearrange the altered word once its L has become a Y.
explanation.definitionFit: To ossify is literally to harden into bone, close to becoming petrified, as remains do when they become fossils.

clue.text: See 19
Drink engulfs bullfighter or missing master painter

indicators.note: to engulf is to swallow up, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: ale is a drink

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: a matador kills the bull in a bullfight
taken as written, then removed
MA, Master of Arts

explanation.surface: A drink swallows a matador, or a great painter goes missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like a conjunction joining two pictures, but it is fodder: the two letters removed from the bullfighter. MA stands for Master of Arts, the university degree.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema was a Victorian artist famous for scenes of ancient Roman life.

clue.text: I came out in a crescent

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a lunette is a crescent-shaped object or window

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or not in place, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone recalls appearing, or emerging, inside a crescent shape.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble's eight characters are Dickens heroines, so no definition is needed. 'I came' is the fodder, not a verb in the surface sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucie Manette is the heroine of Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities, one of the eight characters named in the preamble.

clue.text: See 4
Type of verse inspired by daemon or Hymen

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so the answer is drawn from within the words

parts.note: runs across the three words

explanation.surface: Poetry prompted by a guardian spirit or the Greek god of marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspired by' reads as muse-talk but signals letters drawn from inside the phrase; Hymen is the Greek god of weddings.
explanation.definitionFit: A monorhyme is a poem or stanza in which every line ends on the same rhyme, a recognised verse form.

clue.text: A minute of music

parts.note: surface reading: sixty seconds of a piece, or a written memo
setter's reading: minute as tiny, so the smallest unit of a tune

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'minute' as a span of time and you look for a short piece; read it as 'tiny' and you want the single sound. A minute is also a memo, adding a second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A single sung or played tone is the smallest building block of a melody, and a minute is also a written memo.

clue.text: Look after sailor in well-ordered surroundings — not like us!

definitions.note: a phrase describing a newspaper; the answer is an adjective

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another
surroundings enclose whatever is placed among them

parts.note: tidy means neat, in good order

indicators.note: after means coming later in order, so one piece is placed behind another

parts.note: AB, able seaman
lo, an old word for look!

explanation.surface: A sailor in a tidy place, with a sniffy aside about people unlike ourselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'us' is the Guardian itself, a broadsheet looking down on the tabloid press; the definition only works with that in mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabloidy means in the sensational style of popular newspapers, which a broadsheet like the one printing the puzzle claims not to be.

clue.text: Service flat at little expense

parts.note: a flat surface is even
bought for a song means bought cheaply

explanation.surface: A cheap serviced apartment, like an estate agent's advert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service flat' is a rented apartment in British English, but here the words split: 'Service' is the definition and 'flat' starts the wordplay. The idiom 'for a song' means cheaply.
explanation.definitionFit: Evensong is the Anglican evening prayer service, sung or said in churches and cathedrals.

clue.text: Runner Steve, run!

parts.note: his initial
Steve Cram, the British middle-distance runner and world mile record holder

explanation.surface: A shout urging the athlete Steve to get moving.
explanation.walkthrough: Steve Cram was a British 1500m and mile champion of the 1980s; written as S. Cram, initial plus surname, he gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Scram is a slangy command to go away quickly, the same as telling someone to flee.

clue.text: Bobby at Tate Britain?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a British police officer

definitions.note: a phrase for something hanging in a gallery; the answer is a painter's name
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the English landscape painter whose works hang in that London gallery

explanation.surface: A policeman on duty at a London art gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: A bobby is British slang for a police officer. Tate Britain is a London gallery of British art holding many works by John Constable.
explanation.definitionFit: A constable is the lowest police rank, and John Constable painted The Hay Wain and other English landscapes.

clue.text: Wanting the technique — that would pull the girls?

definitions.text: Wanting the technique — that would pull the girls?

parts.words: Wanting the technique — that would pull the girls?
parts.note: surface reading: someone lacking a seduction method
setter's reading: the proverb says timidity never won a fair lady, so the timid one lacks what wins hearts

explanation.surface: A hapless man without the chat-up skills to attract women.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue leans on the proverb 'faint heart never won fair lady'; to pull is British slang for attracting a romantic partner.
explanation.definitionFit: A timid, cowardly person, the kind the old proverb says will never win a fair lady, so lacks the means to woo.

clue.text: Prominent leader

definitions.note: an adjective; the answer here is a noun, a raised knob
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a stud or knob that sticks out, as on a shield or ceiling
second meaning: the person in charge

explanation.surface: A well-known head of an organisation.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like one noun phrase, but they are separate meanings: a protruding ornament and a person in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is a raised stud, as on a shield's centre, and also an employer or manager who gives orders.

clue.text: Form of army biscuit?

indicators.note: a form of something is a new shape made from the same stuff, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging
a graham cracker is a wholemeal biscuit

explanation.surface: A question about some kind of military ration biscuit.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble's characters need no definition. A graham cracker is a sweet wholemeal biscuit, best known in the US.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Graham is the gentle heroine of Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit, one of the eight characters the preamble refers to.

clue.text: Before boy keeping 5 among sleuths, possibly old hat

indicators.note: before places one piece ahead of the rest
possibly suggests one of several versions, so the letters can be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: Len, a boy's name

indicators.note: to be among things is to sit in their midst, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: the Yard, Scotland Yard, London's police detectives
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: Something about a young detective, possibly with an outdated hat.
explanation.walkthrough: '5' looks like a reference to another answer but is the Roman numeral. 'Old hat' wants to mean unoriginal; 'old' is anagram fodder. Scotland Yard is the London police headquarters, so its detectives are the Yard.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dolly Varden is a wide-brimmed, flower-trimmed lady's hat named after the coquette in Dickens's Barnaby Rudge, herself one of the eight characters.

clue.text: County reduced by oxidisation to a paper

indicators.note: reduced means cut down, so a letter is lost from the end

parts.note: Lincs, the standard short form of Lincolnshire, an English county
rust is iron oxide formed by oxidisation
taken as written

explanation.surface: An English county being worn away by corrosion into a sheet of paper.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincolnshire is an English county in the east Midlands, routinely shortened to Lincs; dropping the S gives LINC.
explanation.definitionFit: Lincrusta is an embossed Victorian wallcovering, a heavy relief wallpaper still used for decorating walls and dados.

clue.text: Publican maybe from another scene in fiction

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another

parts.note: a lie is a fiction, an untruth

indicators.note: another version of something is a different arrangement of it

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: A pub landlord who might have stepped out of a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks the definition as an example: a publican is one kind of licence-holder. In Britain a pub landlord must hold a licence to sell alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: A licensee holds a licence, and the person who runs a pub is a classic example as the licensed seller of alcohol.

clue.text: Bandage holding broken lip, skip as high as permitted — the sky?

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase; the answer is a noun

parts.note: a T-bandage is a T-shaped surgical dressing

indicators.note: to hold is to grip, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: to skip something is to leave it out

indicators.note: something broken has its parts out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging
surface padding that nods to the saying about the sky and limits

explanation.surface: A first-aider dressing a split lip, then a wistful nod to how high one may go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The sky?' alludes to the saying 'the sky's the limit', confirming the definition. The broken lip sits inside the T and OMIT pair, after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A top limit is a ceiling or maximum, the greatest height or amount allowed, which is what the phrase about permission describes.

clue.text: In a manner of speaking, my French and German hardware

indicators.note: in places the following pieces inside another

parts.note: irony is a way of speaking that means the opposite of what is said
mon is French for my
GER, the abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: Speaking loosely, one's French and German tools and fittings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a manner of speaking' wants to be a filler meaning 'so to speak'; 'In' is the container signal and the rest is IRONY.
explanation.definitionFit: Ironmongery is the British word for metal goods such as tools, locks and fittings sold by an ironmonger: hardware.

clue.text: Letters were guide to gold — go slow!

parts.note: Litt., as in D.Litt., Doctor of Letters
led means acted as guide, showed the way
or is gold in heraldry
rit., ritardando, the musical direction to slow down

explanation.surface: Old correspondence that pointed the way to treasure, with a warning to take it easy.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble's characters need no definition. 'Letters' is the scholarly abbreviation, not post; 'go slow' is a musical marking, not an industrial dispute.
explanation.definitionFit: Little Dorrit is Amy Dorrit, title heroine of Dickens's novel set partly in the Marshalsea debtors' prison, one of the eight characters.

clue.text: Set out before her season's in progress

indicators.note: before places one piece ahead of the next
out suggests disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging
taken as written
summer is a season, with its 's kept
something on is happening now

explanation.surface: Someone sets off ahead of a woman while her busy season is under way.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble supplies the definition. Read 'season's' as 'season is': summer's on means summer is under way.
explanation.definitionFit: Esther Summerson is the narrator and heroine of Dickens's Bleak House, one of the eight characters the preamble mentions.

clue.text: See about number after 19

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: a see is a bishop's diocese, and Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: An instruction to check a figure that follows another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After 19' places the answer after LITTLE: Little Em'ly in David Copperfield. 'See' wants to be a verb but is a bishop's seat.
explanation.definitionFit: Little Em'ly is Peggotty's niece in Dickens's David Copperfield, seduced by Steerforth, and one of the preamble's eight characters.

clue.text: Correct wear for the stage?

definitions.note: a phrase describing items; the answer is a plural noun

parts.note: proper means correct, right
ties are worn round the neck

explanation.surface: The right costume for an actor to put on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correct wear' looks like costume, the obvious stage clothing; but the theatre sense of the answer is the objects used on stage, props.
explanation.definitionFit: Properties, usually shortened to props, are the movable objects actors handle in a theatrical production.

clue.text: Fear article in film

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another

parts.note: pic, short for picture, a film
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A piece about fear in cinema, like a horror review.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords 'article' usually means A, AN or THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Panic is sudden overwhelming fright, an intense form of the emotion named in the clue.

clue.text: Last sound to be heard after 19?

indicators.note: what is heard is taken in by the ear, so only pronunciation counts and spelling may differ

parts.note: a knell is the bell tolled at a death or funeral

explanation.surface: The final ringing one hears when something is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After 19' places the answer after LITTLE: Little Nell, whose death in The Old Curiosity Shop famously moved Victorian readers, fitting the funeral bell.
explanation.definitionFit: Little Nell is the child heroine of Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop and one of the eight characters the preamble refers to.

clue.text: See 20
Drawback familiar to film director

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a snag or problem

definitions.note: a phrase; the answer is the nickname itself
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the short pet name of Alfred Hitchcock

explanation.surface: A problem well known to someone who makes movies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Familiar to' looks like 'known to', but it means the familiar or pet form of a name: Alfred Hitchcock was known as Hitch.
explanation.definitionFit: A hitch is a snag that holds things up, and Hitch was the nickname of the British suspense director Alfred Hitchcock.

clue.text: Star in the East?

parts.note: E, the compass point
stella is Latin for star

explanation.surface: The star of Bethlehem seen by the wise men in the east.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the Magi's star in the east; the preamble supplies the definition, so the whole clue is wordplay with East leading.
explanation.definitionFit: Estella is Miss Havisham's cold, beautiful ward in Dickens's Great Expectations, one of the eight characters in the preamble.

clue.text: Fellow politician always fellow?

parts.note: co- is the prefix meaning joint or fellow, as in co-worker
MP, Member of Parliament
e'er, the poetic contraction of ever

explanation.surface: A party colleague who is forever a comrade.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word does two jobs: the first becomes a prefix, the second is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A compeer is an equal or companion, a peer of the same standing, which is one sense of a fellow.
